title: Principal Component Analysis: directions, eigenvalues and explained variance
objectives: Explain PCA as successive orthogonal linear combinations that maximise variance.
Find principal-component directions from eigenvectors of a covariance or correlation matrix.
Calculate eigenvalues, explained variance and cumulative explained variance.
Interpret scores, loadings, scaling choices and repeated eigenvalues.
Solve the June 2026 Paper 2 Q2 equicorrelation problem.

prereq.name: Variance and covariance of linear combinations
prereq.why: PCA maximises the variance of a linear combination, aᵀΣa.

prereq.name: Symmetric matrices and orthogonal eigenvectors
prereq.why: Covariance and correlation matrices are symmetric; their eigenvectors provide orthogonal component directions.

prereq.name: Trace, determinant and characteristic equations
prereq.why: The trace checks eigenvalue sums and the characteristic equation yields eigenvalues.

traps: Eigenvectors give directions; eigenvalues give component variances.
PC1 is a direction, not necessarily one original variable.
PCA scores are uncorrelated, not generally independent.
Covariance PCA is scale-sensitive; correlation PCA standardises variables.
Explained variance divides by the sum of all eigenvalues.

cards: Unit eigenvector of Σ or R
tricks: Try the all-ones vector for an equicorrelation matrix.
Check the eigenvalue sum against the trace.
For a p×p correlation matrix, eigenvalues sum to p.
Repeated eigenvalues identify an eigenspace, not a unique basis.
remember: Eigenvectors are directions; eigenvalues are variances.
Uncorrelated does not automatically mean independent.

howto: Centre the data and decide whether raw scales are meaningful. Form the covariance matrix or, after standardisation, the correlation matrix. Find eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors, order them from largest to smallest, and interpret the eigenvectors as component directions. Each eigenvalue is the variance of its score. Divide by the trace to obtain explained-variance proportions. For June 2026 Q2, use the all-ones vector to obtain the largest eigenvalue, then use the trace to check the remaining eigenvalues.

scenes.title: Three tools before PCA
scenes.objective: Recover variance, covariance and eigenvalue language.
body: PCA summarises several related measurements with a smaller number of new measurements. It searches for directions in which the data vary most.
Variance measures spread. Covariance measures how two variables move together. An eigenvector is a direction preserved by matrix multiplication.
A covariance matrix is symmetric, so its eigenvectors can be chosen orthonormal. This is why standard PCA produces uncorrelated component scores.

refresh: The covariance term records joint movement.
For aX+bY, multiply each variance by the squared coefficient.

items.recall: v is an eigenvector and λ its eigenvalue.
refresh: The vector direction is unchanged by multiplication.
In PCA, λ is the variance along a unit eigenvector.

items.recall: The sum of the original variances and the sum of the eigenvalues.
refresh: Trace is the sum of diagonal entries.
It is a fast check on an eigenvalue calculation.

ask.q: If two variables are positively correlated, what extra term appears in Var(X+Y)?

scenes.title: Why rotate the variables?
scenes.objective: Explain PCA as a rotation that captures shared variation.
body: Imagine measuring height, arm span and leg length. These measurements tend to move together, so much of their variation overlaps.
PCA finds a first score in the direction of greatest spread. A second score is perpendicular to the first and captures the greatest remaining spread. Later scores continue this process.
The first few scores may preserve most variation with fewer numbers. PCA is dimension reduction, not arbitrary variable deletion.

scenario.teaser: Six correlated body measurements; one compact summary.
scenario.title: Compressing a health survey
body: A team records height, weight, waist, hip, arm span and chest circumference for 600 adults. The measurements are correlated. The team wants a smaller set of scores for clustering. Choosing two variables by intuition may discard information. PCA uses the full covariance structure. However, the measurements use different units and scales: kilograms and centimetres. Raw covariance PCA may let larger numerical variances dominate, so the team should consider correlation-matrix PCA after standardisation.
scenario.q: Why might correlation PCA be preferred?
scenario.answer: The variables have different units and scales; standardisation gives each unit variance before extracting components.

ask.q: Does PCA simply select the original variable with the largest variance?
ask.nudge: A component can be a linear combination of several variables.

blocks.body: For centred p-dimensional X, a score in direction a is Z=aᵀX. Its variance is aᵀΣa.
Maximise aᵀΣa subject to aᵀa=1. The solution is a unit eigenvector for the largest eigenvalue λ₁.
The second component maximises variance subject to unit length and perpendicularity to the first. It is an eigenvector for λ₂. Continue in descending order.

blocks.h: Why λ is the score variance
blocks.body: If Σaⱼ=λⱼaⱼ and aⱼᵀaⱼ=1, then Var(aⱼᵀX)=aⱼᵀΣaⱼ=λⱼ.

ask.q: Why constrain a to have unit length?
ask.nudge: Without it, scaling a by 10 would multiply the variance by 100.

scenes.title: Covariance PCA, correlation PCA, scores and loadings
scenes.objective: Choose the input matrix and interpret coefficients.

blocks.body: Use Σ when original scales are meaningful and their variance magnitudes should influence the analysis.
Use R when variables have different units or should begin with equal standardised variance. Since tr(R)=p, its eigenvalues sum to p.
For centred observation x, component score zⱼ=aⱼᵀx. The entries of aⱼ define the component direction.
PC j proportion = λⱼ/Σλᵢ. The first k cumulative proportion is (λ₁+…+λₖ)/Σλᵢ. Retention is a modelling decision; no universal cutoff applies.

ask.q: A variable is in rupees and another in proportions. What should you decide before PCA?
ask.nudge: Is the scale difference substantive or merely a unit choice?

scenes.title: Guided case — how many components?
scenes.objective: Calculate cumulative explained variance and justify a decision.
scenes.problem: Five standardised welfare indicators have eigenvalues 2.5, 1.2, 0.7, 0.4 and 0.2. Find each proportion, the first-two cumulative proportion and interpret retaining two components.
hints: Check the trace: eigenvalues must sum to five.
Divide each eigenvalue by five and add the first two.
Separate the numerical result from the retention decision.
scenes.answer: The proportions are 50%, 24%, 14%, 8% and 4%. The first two explain 74%. Two components reduce five dimensions while retaining 74%; inspect loadings and the importance of omitted variation before deciding.
scenes.check: The eigenvalues sum to five and the proportions sum to 100%.

scenario.teaser: A policy team needs a small dashboard.
scenario.title: A transparent retention decision
body: A state planning team measures school completion, primary-care access, electricity, sanitation and drinking water across districts. The standardised PCA eigenvalues are 2.5, 1.2, 0.7, 0.4 and 0.2. Two components explain 74%. The team should inspect loadings and ensure the remaining 26% does not contain a critical policy signal. A percentage threshold is evidence, not a substitute for interpretation.
scenario.q: What should the team inspect beyond 74%?
scenario.answer: Component loadings, substantive meaning and whether omitted components contain important policy information.

solution.why: Two components retain 74% of total standardised variation.

scenes.title: Six common traps
scenes.objective: Distinguish valid PCA facts from overstatements.

items.claim: The first PC is always an original variable.
items.why: It is generally a linear combination.
A covariance matrix is positive semidefinite.
The covariance matrix is diagonal in the PC basis.
Not in general; joint normality is a sufficient additional condition.

items.claim: Eigenvalues of a p×p correlation matrix sum to one.
A repeated eigenvalue need not have a unique eigenvector basis.
items.why: Any orthonormal basis of that eigenspace is valid.

scenes.title: Transfer — scale-sensitive PCA
scenes.problem: Income in thousands has variance 400; satisfaction on a 0–10 scale has variance 4; their correlation is 0.6. Explain why covariance and correlation PCA may differ. Find the correlation-matrix eigenvalues.
hints: Write the correlation matrix with unit diagonal.
scenes.answer: The covariance is 0.6×20×2=24, giving Σ=[[400,24],[24,4]], where income's scale dominates. Correlation PCA uses R=[[1,0.6],[0.6,1]], with eigenvalues 1.6 and 0.4 and directions (1,1)/√2 and (1,−1)/√2.
scenes.check: The eigenvalues sum to trace 2 and are non-negative.

scenes.title: Interpretation and limitations
scenes.objective: Explain what PCA does and does not establish.

blocks.body: Eigenvector coefficients describe a component direction; they are not regression coefficients or causal effects.
If a is an eigenvector, −a is also one. Reversing all signs reverses the score but not its variance.
The eigenspace is identified, but its orthonormal basis is not unique.
PCA is a linear variance summary. It does not guarantee prediction, causal interpretation, cluster separation or preservation of low-variance scientific signals.

ask.q: If all loadings change sign, does explained variance change?
ask.nudge: The score changes sign but its variance does not.

items.q: Eigenvalue sum for p×p correlation matrix?

items.a: λⱼ divided by the sum of all eigenvalues.

items.q: Why is the all-ones vector an eigenvector of an equicorrelation matrix?
items.a: Each row has the same sum.

items.q: What does a repeated eigenvalue imply?
items.a: The eigenspace is identified but its basis is not unique.
